subtopics.title: Meaning and branches
subtopics.content:
Agriculture is the science, art and business of producing plants and animals and using agricultural resources to provide food, fibre, raw materials and other products. Major branches include crop husbandry, animal husbandry, horticulture, soil science, agricultural engineering, forestry, wildlife management and agribusiness. These branches are interdependent: soil fertility affects crops, crop residues can feed livestock, manure can improve soils, forests protect catchments, and marketing determines whether production is profitable.

EXAM AND PRACTICAL APPLICATION

When answering an examination question on this subtopic, begin with the
exact agricultural concept being tested. If the question asks for a
process, present the steps in logical order. If it asks for an explanation,
connect the practice to its biological, physical or economic reason. Where
appropriate, identify advantages, limitations, safety issues, costs and
environmental effects.

PRACTICAL APPROACH

In practical work, identify the material or specimen accurately, state the
apparatus or method, record observations before drawing conclusions, use
appropriate units and repeat measurements where necessary. Keep controlled
variables constant when investigating a relationship. Anomalous results
should be considered rather than automatically removed.

ZIMBABWE APPLICATION

Agricultural decisions should reflect local rainfall, soil, available
resources, labour, markets and farming systems. Indigenous knowledge can
contribute useful observations and practices, but claims should be evaluated
using evidence, safety and sustainability. The best management practice is
not necessarily the most expensive one; it is the one that solves the stated
problem effectively within the available resources.

subtopics.title: Importance of agriculture to Zimbabwe
subtopics.content:
Agriculture contributes to food security, employment, household income, industrial raw materials, export earnings and rural development. It supports industries supplying fertiliser, seed, machinery, packaging, transport and processing. Sustainable agriculture aims to meet present needs while maintaining soil, water, biodiversity and productive capacity. Production is affected by rainfall, drought, pests, disease, input prices, infrastructure, finance and markets.

subtopics.content:
Land may be used for crops, livestock, forestry, wildlife, settlement, infrastructure and conservation. Choice depends on soil, climate, relief, water, vegetation, population, technology, markets, labour, capital and tenure. Physical limitations include steep slopes, shallow soils, low rainfall, waterlogging and salinity; human limitations include finance, labour, transport and market access.

subtopics.title: Land tenure
subtopics.content:
Land tenure describes the system under which land is held, occupied and used. It influences security, investment, access to finance and long-term planning. Secure tenure can encourage investments such as orchards, fencing, irrigation and conservation structures because benefits may extend over many seasons. Tenure should be distinguished from land quality and land size.

subtopics.title: Crop rotation
subtopics.content:
Crop rotation is the planned sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons. A good rotation can interrupt pest and disease cycles, distribute nutrient demand, improve soil structure and include legumes that contribute nitrogen through biological fixation. Rotation planning considers crop family, rooting depth, nutrient demand, residues, weeds, water and market value.

subtopics.content:
A farm plan locates fields, livestock areas, buildings, roads, water points, grazing areas and conservation structures. Planning should consider slope, drainage, prevailing wind, access, security, livestock movement, biosecurity and future expansion. Roads should connect important points efficiently without creating unnecessary erosion channels.

subtopics.content:
Climatic factors include rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and sunshine. Soil factors include depth, texture, structure, fertility, pH and drainage. Biotic factors include weeds, pests, diseases, beneficial organisms and competition. Farmers can modify some factors through irrigation, drainage, mulching, windbreaks, fertilisation and protected cultivation, but every intervention has costs and possible environmental effects.

subtopics.title: Rainfall: distribution, reliability, effectiveness and intensity
subtopics.content:
Rainfall matters because crops need water for germination, photosynthesis, nutrient transport and growth. Distribution concerns timing through the season; reliability concerns consistency between seasons; effectiveness concerns the amount actually available after runoff, evaporation and drainage; intensity concerns how quickly rain falls. Heavy intense rainfall may increase runoff and erosion rather than infiltration.

subtopics.title: Natural farming regions of Zimbabwe
subtopics.content:
Zimbabwe has contrasting agro-ecological conditions. Rainfall, temperature, altitude, soils and growing-season length influence suitable crops and livestock. Drier areas require stronger drought and water-management strategies, while wetter areas may support broader crop choices but can face erosion, leaching and disease pressure. Recommendations should match local conditions rather than treating the country as climatically uniform.

subtopics.title: Natural disasters and risk management
subtopics.content:
Agriculture is exposed to drought, floods, storms, veld fires, pest outbreaks and disease. Risk management includes preparedness, prevention, response and recovery. Measures include water storage, fodder reserves, seed reserves, early-warning information, insurance, drainage, fire management, soil conservation and diversification. Recovery should restore production while reducing future vulnerability.

subtopics.content:
Forests provide timber, fuelwood, poles, fruits, medicines, wildlife habitat, carbon storage and catchment protection. Hardwood and softwood species have different properties and uses. Sustainable forestry maintains regeneration and avoids harvesting faster than forests can recover. Fire, illegal cutting and overgrazing can reduce forest productivity.

subtopics.title: Deforestation and control
subtopics.content:
Deforestation is removal of forest cover faster than regeneration. Causes include agricultural expansion, settlement, fuelwood, charcoal, timber harvesting and uncontrolled fires. Effects include habitat loss, biodiversity decline, erosion, altered water movement and reduced carbon storage. Control includes afforestation, reforestation, agro-forestry, controlled harvesting, fire management and community participation.

subtopics.title: Agro-forestry
subtopics.content:

Systems include boundary planting, woodlots and silvopastoral systems. Species selection must consider competition for water and nutrients, shade, roots, market value and climate.

Sustainable utilisation requires populations and habitats to remain productive. Protected areas, monitoring, laws, community participation and indigenous knowledge can support conservation.

subtopics.title: Human-wildlife conflict
subtopics.content:
Conflict can occur when wildlife damages crops, kills livestock, competes for water or threatens people. Habitat loss, settlement near wildlife areas and drought can increase conflict. Measures include secure fencing, guarding, deterrents, livestock protection, early warning, land-use planning and regulated problem-animal control. Conservation and community safety should be considered together.

subtopics.title: Weathering and soil formation
subtopics.content:
Soil develops from parent material through physical, chemical and biological weathering plus accumulation and decomposition of organic matter. Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces; chemical weathering changes minerals through reactions with water, oxygen and acids; biological activity by roots and organisms contributes to breakdown. Climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time influence formation.

subtopics.content:
Agricultural soil contains mineral particles, organic matter, soil water, soil air and living organisms. Mineral particles form the framework; organic matter improves aggregation and nutrient supply; soil water carries dissolved nutrients; soil air supplies oxygen for roots and aerobic organisms. The balance of components affects fertility, drainage and root growth.

subtopics.title: Soil organisms and humus
subtopics.content:
Bacteria, fungi, earthworms and other organisms decompose residues and contribute to nutrient cycling and structure. Humus is relatively stable organic material formed during decomposition. It improves aggregation, water-holding capacity and nutrient availability. Good management retains residues and organic inputs.

subtopics.title: Soil texture
subtopics.content:
Texture is the relative proportion of sand, silt and clay. Sandy soils drain rapidly and hold less water and nutrients. Clay soils have high surface area and water and nutrient retention but may drain slowly and be difficult to work when wet. Loams provide a useful balance for many crops. Texture can be estimated by feel or measured by particle-size analysis.

subtopics.content:

Organic matter, roots and biological activity encourage stable aggregates. Compaction, excessive cultivation, erosion and loss of organic matter can destroy structure. Conservation tillage and organic inputs help maintain it.

subtopics.content:

Topsoil usually has more organic matter and biological activity; subsoil may contain materials moved downward from above. Profile study considers colour, texture, structure, roots, stones and depth.

subtopics.content:

Roots require both water and oxygen, so prolonged saturation can restrict respiration while insufficient water causes stress and wilting. Texture and structure strongly affect infiltration and drainage.

subtopics.content:

Erosion reduces topsoil, nutrients and organic matter and may cause sedimentation of waterways. Conservation includes contouring, grass strips, terraces, mulching, cover crops, minimum tillage and controlled grazing.

Deficiency diagnosis should use symptoms, soil tests and crop history.

Symbiotic bacteria in root nodules of suitable legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen into biologically useful forms. Rotation and residues improve nutrient cycling. Legumes still require careful pest, disease, weed and harvest management.

subtopics.content:

Non-ruminants such as pigs and poultry have different digestive systems and generally depend less on microbial fibre digestion. The distinction affects feeding and management.

subtopics.content:

The crop stores feed, the proventriculus secretes digestive substances and the gizzard mechanically grinds feed.

Sudden diet changes can cause digestive problems.

subtopics.content:

Fixed costs do not vary directly with short-term output, such as some buildings and machinery. Gross margin helps compare enterprises, but full profitability requires consideration of fixed and other costs.

subtopics.content:

Fertiliser may initially raise yield strongly, but beyond an optimum each extra application may add little output or cause damage. Economic efficiency matters more than maximum input use.

A simple break-even quantity can be estimated as fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, where contribution equals selling price minus variable cost per unit. Sensitivity analysis shows the effect of changes in yield, price or input cost.

subtopics.content:
For a crop-production essay, organise the answer from planning through marketing: site and climate requirements; land preparation; seed or planting material; planting; nutrition; water; weeds; pests and diseases; routine management; harvesting; post-harvest handling; marketing; records; and environmental considerations. Explain why and when operations are done rather than listing them.

When answering an examination question on this subtopic, begin with the
exact agricultural concept being tested. If the question asks for a
process, present the steps in logical order. If it asks for an explanation,
connect the practice to its biological, physical or economic reason. Where
appropriate, identify advantages, limitations, safety issues, costs and
environmental effects.
